case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court’s denial of a federal contractor’s “derivative sovereign immunity” defense at the summary-judgment stage is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (appellate jurisdiction over “final decisions” of district courts) and the judge-made collateral-order doctrine construing § 1291.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor is sued for performing the federal government’s delegated, authorized work, and therefore a denial of that protection should be immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine; otherwise, contractors lose the core benefit of the doctrine (avoiding litigation burdens and the chilling effect on government contracting) because the right cannot be effectively vindicated after final judgment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that a denial of derivative sovereign immunity is not a classic “immunity from suit” warranting interlocutory appeal but instead is a merits-related defense (turning on whether the contractor acted within valid government authority and complied with federal directions), making it unsuitable for collateral-order review; allowing immediate appeals would expand the narrow collateral-order doctrine, increase piecemeal litigation, and § 1291’s final-judgment rule already provides adequate review after final judgment.
key_precedents: Combs v. (Kentucky blasting case) (52 S.W.2d 717/720) (state-law example treating contractor as agent of the sovereign when acting non-negligently)
Nelson (Minnesota Supreme Court bridge/blasting case) (state-law example describing contractor as the State’s agent and tying liability to the State’s duty/authority)
CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari, 141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (cert-stage reference; Court previously sought SG views on the same collateral-order question)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy: if Yearsley is an immunity from suit, its benefit is lost without immediate appeal. But Justice Kagan’s emphasis that Yearsley turns on validly conferred federal authority and compliance with federal directions—often disputed, fact-bound, and merits-adjacent—means the order generally fails Cohen’s “completely separate from the merits” requirement and runs straight into Johnson v. Jones’s bar on interlocutory review of fact-intensive entitlement disputes. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Mohawk reinforces my minimalist view that we should not create a new collateral-order category where post-judgment review suffices and litigation burdens alone do not make the right “effectively unreviewable.” A narrow, institution-protective disposition is to hold no collateral-order jurisdiction at least when the denial rests on contested authorization/compliance facts, leaving for another day any purely legal denial in a different posture.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—pressed in Mitchell terms—is that Yearsley is an immunity from suit and so must be immediately appealable, but that label cannot override § 1291’s textual limitation to “final decisions” and our insistence that Cohen remain narrow. As Justice Kagan explains, Yearsley turns on whether authority was validly conferred and whether the contractor complied with federal directions—questions often intertwined with the merits and fact-bound in the Johnson v. Jones sense, defeating Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald reinforces that Yearsley is conditional (authority-and-instructions), not a categorical constitutional immunity whose value is necessarily destroyed by trial; any error can be corrected after final judgment under Hallock/Mohawk’s understanding that litigation burdens alone do not make an order “effectively unreviewable.” If Congress wishes to authorize interlocutory appeals for contractor defenses, it may do so; we should not expand a judge-made exception beyond the original meaning of § 1291’s final-judgment rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell-style label of Yearsley as an “immunity from suit,” but that characterization cannot satisfy Cohen’s separate-from-the-merits and effectively-unreviewable requirements. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Yearsley turns on whether authority was validly conferred and whether the contractor complied with federal directions—questions commonly intertwined with the merits and fact-bound in the Johnson v. Jones sense, making collateral-order review a poor fit. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Mohawk is also persuasive under a restrained, textualist view of § 1291: ordinary litigation burdens do not justify expanding a narrow judge-made exception when post-judgment appeal can correct error. Given the practical consequence of inviting routine piecemeal appeals in contractor litigation, I see no basis to recognize collateral-order jurisdiction here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—pressed most plausibly through the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy—is that Yearsley should be treated as an immunity from suit and therefore immediately appealable. But Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Cohen’s “completely separate from the merits” requirement is decisive for me: Yearsley turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and complied with federal directions, which is commonly fact-bound and merits-adjacent in the Johnson v. Jones sense. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett underscore via Will v. Hallock and Mohawk, we must keep collateral-order review “narrow and selective,” and ordinary litigation burdens do not make the denial “effectively unreviewable” because an erroneous denial can be remedied after final judgment. Pragmatically, recognizing interlocutory appeals here would invite delay and piecemeal review that disproportionately harms plaintiffs seeking redress, without satisfying Cohen’s stringent limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—pressed in the Chief Justice’s framing—is to treat Yearsley as an immunity from suit akin to Mitchell, but that label doesn’t satisfy Cohen’s separateness and effective-unreviewability requirements when the entitlement turns on authorization-and-compliance facts. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize through Mohawk and Will v. Hallock, ordinary litigation burdens do not justify expanding our “narrow and selective” collateral-order doctrine where post-judgment review remains available to correct error. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald reinforces my view that Yearsley is conditional and merits-adjacent, making these denials look like the fact-bound disputes Johnson v. Jones says are poor candidates for interlocutory appeal. Institutionally and textually (as Justice Thomas notes with § 1291), creating a new appeal-as-of-right category here would invite routine piecemeal appeals without a clear doctrinal hook.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy: if Yearsley were a true immunity from suit, delay until final judgment would forfeit its core benefit. But as Justice Kagan explains, Yearsley/Campbell-Ewald makes the contractor’s protection conditional on validly conferred authority and compliance with federal directions—an inquiry typically entangled with merits facts, failing Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement and fitting Johnson v. Jones’s bar on interlocutory review of fact-bound disputes. Justice Thomas’s reliance on § 1291’s text and Will v. Hallock reinforces that we should not enlarge a judge-made exception absent a clear historical analogue or congressional authorization, and Mohawk confirms that ordinary litigation burdens do not render an order “effectively unreviewable.” Post-judgment review can correct any error without opening the door to piecemeal appeals in routine contractor cases.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy—branding Yearsley as an immunity from suit such that the right is lost absent immediate appeal—but, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Yearsley inquiry is typically conditional on validly conferred authority and compliance with federal directions, which is often fact-bound and merits-entangled and thus fails Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement in the Johnson v. Jones sense. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Mohawk is also persuasive: litigation burdens alone do not make an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment where ordinary appellate review can correct error. Institutionally and as a matter of § 1291’s final-judgment rule, recognizing a new collateral-order category here would invite routine piecemeal appeals in contractor cases without a historically grounded or congressionally authorized basis. I therefore remain with the Respondent, at least where—like here—the denial turns on disputed authorization/compliance facts rather than a purely legal issue.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy—that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose value is lost without immediate appeal—but Justice Kagan correctly emphasizes that Yearsley turns on conditional, often fact-bound questions of valid federal authorization and compliance with federal directions, which are commonly merits-entangled and thus fail Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about Johnson v. Jones further reinforces that interlocutory review is especially inappropriate where the denial rests on disputed facts about authorization/compliance, because that invites piecemeal appeals over the very matters bound up with liability. And as Justice Thomas notes, § 1291’s text and Will v. Hallock/Mohawk counsel a “narrow and selective” collateral-order doctrine; ordinary litigation burdens are not enough to make the order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment when errors can be corrected on ordinary appeal. I therefore see no doctrinally legitimate basis to recognize a new collateral-order category for Yearsley denials in this posture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—pressed through the Mitchell v. Forsyth analogy—is that Yearsley is an immunity-from-suit whose value is lost if litigation proceeds, but that characterization cannot do the work Cohen requires here. As Justice Kagan explains, Yearsley typically turns on whether authority was validly conferred and whether the contractor complied with federal directions, which is often merits- and fact-entangled and thus fails Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement and triggers Johnson v. Jones’s warning against interlocutory review of fact-bound entitlement disputes. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Mohawk reinforces that ordinary discovery/trial burdens rarely make an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, and the institutional costs of piecemeal contractor appeals are substantial. On a pragmatic, procedure-focused view, the post-judgment appeal remains an adequate corrective while preserving § 1291’s final-judgment rule absent congressional expansion.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and this Court has repeatedly treated the collateral-order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. as a “narrow” and “select” exception to be kept within strict limits. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, Yearsley-style “derivative sovereign immunity” typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with federal directions—issues intertwined with the merits and often fact-bound in the manner Johnson v. Jones held unsuitable for interlocutory appeal. Because the claimed protection can be reviewed after final judgment, and expanding collateral-order review here would invite piecemeal appeals with significant institutional costs, the denial at summary judgment is not immediately appealable under § 1291 as construed by Cohen.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291 grants jurisdiction over only “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judge-made exception that should not be expanded beyond its historically accepted categories. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, derivative sovereign immunity for contractors turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and followed government directions—questions that are often fact-bound and intertwined with the merits, making interlocutory review ill-suited under Johnson v. Jones. Will v. Hallock cautions that collateral-order review must remain “stringent” to prevent piecemeal appeals, and any broader interlocutory regime for contractor defenses should come from Congress, not judicial invention. Because the defense can be reviewed after final judgment and does not categorically confer a sovereign’s constitutional immunity from suit like the Eleventh Amendment cases, § 1291’s final-judgment rule should control.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1291’s text establishes a strong final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception that applies only when an order conclusively resolves an important issue completely separate from the merits and is effectively unreviewable after final judgment under Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. Whether Yearsley applies typically turns on merits-entangled questions—e.g., whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with governmental directions—so it is not “completely separate from the merits.” Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as limiting liability when a contractor acts pursuant to validly conferred authority, not as a freestanding immunity from suit akin to qualified immunity, and any error can ordinarily be corrected on appeal after final judgment. Expanding collateral-order review here would invite piecemeal appeals in routine contractor cases, undermining § 1291’s practical function and the Court’s repeated insistence that collateral-order appeals remain tightly confined.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule and this Court’s “narrow and selective” collateral-order doctrine counsel against creating a new category of interlocutory appeals for Yearsley-style derivative sovereign immunity, which is often bound up with whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and complied with government directions. Under Cohen and Will v. Hallock, the question must be effectively unreviewable after final judgment and sufficiently separate from the merits; here, unlike Mitchell v. Forsyth’s qualified-immunity appeal (a true immunity from suit), the derivative-immunity inquiry typically overlaps merits facts and thus risks piecemeal litigation. Johnson v. Jones further warns that interlocutory review is inappropriate where the dispute turns on fact-intensive determinations rather than a pure legal entitlement to avoid trial. Because contractors can obtain full review after final judgment—and broadening collateral-order review would delay relief for vulnerable plaintiffs and impede access to justice—the denial should not be immediately appealable.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only the narrow Cohen collateral-order exception, which requires (among other things) an issue “completely separate from the merits” and “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment. A Yearsley defense turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and complied with the Government’s directions—questions intertwined with merits and therefore unlike the true “immunity from suit” recognized for qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth. And because an erroneous denial of Yearsley protection can be remedied on appeal after final judgment (as with most defenses to liability), recognizing interlocutory review would expand the collateral-order doctrine contrary to Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter’s admonition to keep it “narrow and selective.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 authorizes appeals only from “final decisions,” and this Court has repeatedly emphasized that the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception that does not permit interlocutory review merely because an asserted defense is important or might be lost absent immediate appeal. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. framed the contractor’s protection as turning on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority and followed the Government’s directions—an inquiry bound up with the merits rather than a freestanding “immunity from suit” like qualified immunity. Because review after final judgment can still fully correct an erroneous denial (and because expanding Cohen risks piecemeal appellate litigation contrary to § 1291’s design), the denial is not immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine. Campbell-Ewald confirms Yearsley’s conditional, authority-and-instructions nature, reinforcing that this is not the sort of categorical immunity warranting interlocutory appeal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies Congress’s strong final-judgment rule, and our judge-made collateral-order doctrine remains “narrow,” “stringent,” and of “modest scope,” with the Court repeatedly declining invitations to expand it. Under Cohen’s three-part test as applied in cases like Digital Equipment and Mohawk, a denial of derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically is not “completely separate from the merits” because it turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and followed federal directions. And unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth—an established immunity from suit for public officials—the Yearsley-style defense is more merits-bound and can be adequately reviewed after final judgment, making it not “effectively unreviewable” in the Cohen sense. Given precedent and practical workability concerns about piecemeal appeals, the better reading is that such denials are not immediately appealable under § 1291’s collateral-order doctrine.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291’s text limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception reserved for orders that conclusively decide an important issue separate from the merits and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment. See Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter, 558 U.S. 100 (2009); Will v. Hallock, 546 U.S. 345 (2006). A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and followed federal directions, making it intertwined with the merits rather than a freestanding entitlement not to stand trial like qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511 (1985). Because errors can be remedied on appeal after final judgment and expanding collateral-order review would undermine § 1291’s final-judgment rule with piecemeal appeals, the denial is not immediately appealable.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule and this Court’s modern collateral-order cases instruct that interlocutory review must remain a “narrow” exception, not a vehicle for piecemeal appeals. Under Cohen’s stringent three-part test as applied in cases like Mohawk Industries, a denial of derivative sovereign immunity at summary judgment typically is not “completely separate from the merits,” because it turns on fact- and merits-bound questions about the scope of delegated authority and compliance with federal directions. Nor is it “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment in the way true immunities from suit are, since any error can be corrected on appeal and litigation burdens alone generally do not justify expanding collateral-order jurisdiction. Preserving procedural regularity and avoiding appellate fragmentation best accords with § 1291’s structure and the Court’s repeated admonition to keep the collateral-order doctrine modest in scope.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court’s pretrial denial of a federal contractor’s claim of “derivative sovereign immunity” is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine rather than only after final judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (appellate jurisdiction over “final decisions”), as interpreted through the Supreme Court’s collateral-order doctrine.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor acts as the government’s agent within the scope of federal authorization, and that the benefits of that immunity—avoiding discovery, trial, and litigation burdens that interfere with federal contracting and governmental functions—are lost if review must wait until after final judgment; therefore, an order denying derivative sovereign immunity should qualify as a collateral order subject to immediate interlocutory appeal.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Menocal and the other respondents contend that so-called derivative sovereign immunity is not a true immunity from being haled into court comparable to qualified immunity or sovereign immunity, but instead is a merits defense (often fact-bound) about whether the contractor acted within valid federal authority and complied with federal directions; because it is intertwined with the merits and can be effectively reviewed after final judgment, the collateral-order doctrine does not permit immediate appeal from its denial, and allowing such appeals would expand interlocutory review beyond the narrow limits of § 1291.
key_precedents: Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940)
CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari, 141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (cert. dismissal/invited SG brief noted in U.S. amicus discussion)
Combs v. (Kentucky case cited as) 52 S.W.2d 720 (blasting/contractor as agent of the Commonwealth—state-law derivative immunity concept referenced by amici)
Nelson (Minnesota Supreme Court case referenced by amici concerning blasting/bridge construction and contractor as agent of the state)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is functional: if Yearsley is “derivative sovereign immunity,” its value is avoiding litigation burdens, so denial should be immediately appealable like qualified immunity. But as Justice Kagan stresses via Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock, Cohen demands a stringent, category-level showing of separability and effective unreviewability, and Yearsley’s “authority validly conferred”/“did not exceed” inquiry is typically fact-bound and merits-adjacent rather than completely separate. Campbell-Ewald, which several colleagues (including Justice Barrett) emphasize, further undermines the immunity-from-suit analogy by rejecting any categorical contractor sharing of the Government’s sovereign immunity, leaving Yearsley as a defense to liability/authority that can be vindicated after final judgment. Recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would risk broad piecemeal appeals in ordinary government-contract litigation, contrary to § 1291 and our repeated admonitions to keep Cohen modest.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best contention is that Yearsley operates as an immunity from suit whose benefits are lost absent immediate appeal, but § 1291’s text confines our jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and Cohen’s exception remains historically narrow. Justice Barrett is right that collateral-order review is reserved for a category of rights “not to stand trial altogether,” whereas Yearsley turns on whether the contractor acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not exceed it—an inquiry often fact-bound and intertwined with the merits, failing Cohen’s separability requirement. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald further weakens the analogy to sovereign or qualified immunity by rejecting any categorical contractor entitlement to share the Government’s immunity from suit. Because an erroneous denial of Yearsley can be corrected after final judgment, it is not “effectively unreviewable” in the stringent sense demanded by Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that Yearsley is “derivative sovereign immunity” and thus a right not to endure litigation—still fails under our collateral-order precedents because the asserted protection turns on whether the contractor stayed within “authority validly conferred,” a merits-adjacent, often fact-bound inquiry. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald is especially telling: if contractors do not categorically share the Government’s immunity, Yearsley looks like a defense conditioned on compliance with federal authorization, not an absolute immunity-from-suit that is irretrievably lost absent immediate appeal. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock confirms we assess the category of orders and keep Cohen’s exception small; recognizing interlocutory review here would invite routine piecemeal appeals in ordinary contracting disputes. Any error in denying Yearsley can be corrected after final judgment, so the denial is not “effectively unreviewable” in the sense § 1291 and our cases require.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is the functional one: if Yearsley is truly an immunity from suit, the protection is lost once a contractor is forced through discovery and trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts notes, Campbell-Ewald rejects any categorical extension of the Government’s sovereign immunity to contractors, which makes Yearsley look less like a freestanding entitlement not to stand trial and more like a merits-adjacent authorization defense. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett are also right that our collateral-order doctrine (Digital Equipment; Will v. Hallock; Mohawk) demands a category-level showing of separability and effective unreviewability, and Yearsley’s “authority validly conferred”/“did not exceed” inquiry is commonly fact-bound and intertwined with the underlying claims. Given the concrete costs of delay to vulnerable plaintiffs, expanding interlocutory appeals here would undercut access to justice without satisfying Cohen’s stringent requirements, and any error can be remedied after final judgment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell-style framing: if Yearsley is truly an immunity from suit, its value is lost without immediate appeal. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Campbell-Ewald rejects the premise that contractors categorically share the Government’s sovereign immunity, which makes Yearsley look like an authorization/merits defense rather than a freestanding entitlement not to stand trial. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock is also decisive for me: Cohen demands a category-level showing of separability and effective unreviewability, and Yearsley’s “validly conferred authority” and “did not exceed it” inquiries are typically fact-bound and merits-adjacent, making post-judgment review adequate in the relevant doctrinal sense. Pragmatically and textually, expanding collateral-order jurisdiction here would predictably open a broad new lane of piecemeal appeals across federal contracting, in tension with § 1291’s final-judgment rule and our repeated insistence on keeping Cohen’s exception small.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument is functional: treating Yearsley as an immunity from suit whose benefits are irretrievably lost if the contractor must litigate. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Campbell-Ewald rejects the premise that contractors categorically share the Government’s sovereign immunity, and Yearsley itself conditions protection on whether the contractor acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not exceed it—an inquiry that is often merits-adjacent and fact-bound. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock reinforces that Cohen’s collateral-order exception must be assessed at the category level and kept “stringent,” and this category would predictably invite routine piecemeal appeals in ordinary government-contract cases. Because an erroneous denial can be corrected after final judgment and the asserted interest is not a clearly established “right not to stand trial,” § 1291’s final-decision rule controls.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that Yearsley’s “derivative sovereign immunity” should be treated like an immunity from suit whose denial is immediately appealable under Mitchell—still falters under our stringent collateral-order framework. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Campbell-Ewald rejects any categorical notion that contractors share the Government’s sovereign immunity, which weakens the claimed “right not to stand trial” and makes Yearsley look like an authority/compliance defense. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Will v. Hallock and Mohawk is decisive for me: we evaluate the category of orders, and Yearsley denials commonly turn on fact-bound questions about whether authority was validly conferred and exceeded, which are intertwined with the merits and reviewable after final judgment. Recognizing interlocutory jurisdiction here would invite broad piecemeal appeals in routine government-contract disputes, undermining § 1291’s final-judgment rule without the kind of historically grounded immunity-from-suit right our precedents require.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Yearsley supplies an immunity-from-suit whose value is lost absent immediate review, but that framing is weakened by Campbell-Ewald (as Chief Justice Roberts stresses) and by Yearsley’s own conditional inquiry into whether the contractor acted within “authority validly conferred,” which is frequently fact-bound and merits-adjacent. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock reinforces that collateral-order review demands a category-wide showing of separability and effective unreviewability, not merely the ordinary burdens of litigation in a given case. Because Yearsley denials can be corrected on appeal after final judgment and recognizing interlocutory jurisdiction here would predictably broaden piecemeal appeals across government-contract disputes, I do not see a textual or precedential basis to expand Cohen’s “small class” of collateral orders. The opposing argument is not strong enough to convert this defense into a clear “right not to stand trial” of the kind Mitchell recognized for qualified immunity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the functional claim that Yearsley is an immunity whose core value is avoiding litigation burdens, but that framing collapses under Cohen because the entitlement asserted is not categorically separate from the merits and is ordinarily reviewable after final judgment. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald is especially persuasive in showing that contractors do not automatically share the Government’s sovereign immunity, weakening the Mitchell-style “right not to stand trial” analogy that would justify interlocutory review. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Digital Equipment and Will v. Hallock reinforces that we assess the category of orders, and Yearsley denials frequently turn on fact-bound questions about the scope of “validly conferred” authority and whether it was exceeded—precisely the sort of merits-adjacent inquiry Cohen’s separability prong is meant to exclude. Given the systemic costs of delay and piecemeal appeals in a broad swath of contractor litigation, I see no doctrinally sound basis to expand collateral-order jurisdiction here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only a “small class” of collateral orders, and we have repeatedly refused to expand that doctrine beyond true immunities from suit. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as a merits/authority defense—whether the contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization—rather than an immunity conferring a right not to stand trial; Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez confirms contractors do not share the Government’s sovereign immunity. Because denial of a Yearsley defense is intertwined with the merits and can be reviewed effectively after final judgment, it does not satisfy the collateral-order doctrine as applied in our immunity cases like Mitchell v. Forsyth. Allowing immediate appeals here would invite broad, disruptive interlocutory review across federal contracting, undermining § 1291’s rule and institutional interests in efficient, orderly adjudication.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291 confers jurisdiction only over “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow exception that this Court has repeatedly refused to expand beyond orders that conclusively determine an important issue wholly separate from the merits and that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. The so-called “derivative sovereign immunity” described in Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as a limitation on liability when a contractor acts pursuant to “authority validly conferred” by the Federal Government, a determination that commonly turns on whether the contractor stayed within the scope of federal authorization and directions—issues intertwined with the merits and fact-bound. Unlike true immunities from suit (e.g., sovereign or qualified immunity), a Yearsley defense can be vindicated on appeal after final judgment, so denial of it does not satisfy § 1291’s collateral-order requirements. Adhering to the text of § 1291 and the historically limited scope of collateral-order review, I would hold the denial not immediately appealable.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1291’s “final decisions” rule admits only a narrow collateral-order exception, and the order here does not qualify because the Yearsley doctrine is best understood as a defense to liability, not a true immunity from suit. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. ties the contractor’s protection to whether it acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not “exceed[] that authority,” inquiries that are commonly intertwined with the merits and often fact-bound, making interlocutory review inconsistent with Cohen’s requirement of separability. This Court has also indicated that contractors do not categorically share the Government’s own immunity from suit, undermining GEO’s analogy to qualified immunity and similar immediately appealable immunities. Allowing immediate appeals whenever a contractor loses a Yearsley motion would substantially expand collateral-order appeals beyond §1291’s practical limits, with significant systemic costs given the breadth of federal contracting.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291’s collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception, and GEO has not shown that a denial of Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” is effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as an authorization/merits defense—whether the contractor acted pursuant to validly conferred federal authority and within the Government’s directions—rather than a true immunity from suit comparable to sovereign or qualified immunity. Because that inquiry is frequently fact-bound and intertwined with the merits, immediate appeal would expand interlocutory review beyond § 1291 and risk delaying remedies for vulnerable plaintiffs whose claims (including forced-labor allegations) deserve timely adjudication. Any error can be corrected on appeal after final judgment without converting this contractor defense into a categorical entitlement to avoid trial and discovery.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only a “small class” of collateral orders, and we have repeatedly insisted the doctrine remain “stringent” and of “modest scope.” Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994); Will v. Hallock, 546 U.S. 345, 350 (2006). A Yearsley defense typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and complied with federal directions, making the issue fact-bound and intertwined with the merits rather than “completely separate” under Cohen/Van Cauwenberghe. And unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511 (1985), Yearsley is not clearly established as an immunity from suit whose value is irretrievably lost absent immediate appeal; erroneous denials can be effectively reviewed after final judgment without expanding interlocutory appeals beyond § 1291’s narrow limits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291’s text authorizes appeals only from “final decisions,” and this Court has repeatedly insisted the collateral-order doctrine remain a “narrow exception” not to be expanded by analogy. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. describes a merits limitation on liability when a contractor acted pursuant to valid federal authorization and direction, a determination commonly bound up with disputed facts and the merits, so it fails Cohen’s requirement that the issue be “completely separate” and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. This Court has also rejected the premise that Yearsley confers the sovereign’s own immunity from suit on contractors, see Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez, which undercuts any claim to an immediately appealable “right not to stand trial.” Allowing interlocutory appeals here would invite routine mid-litigation appeals in a vast range of contract cases, contrary to § 1291’s separation-of-powers-respecting final-judgment rule and our collateral-order precedents.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and our collateral-order doctrine remains “narrow” and “stringent,” lest it “swallow” that rule. Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994); Mohawk Indus., Inc. v. Carpenter, 558 U.S. 100, 106-07 (2009). A denial of Yearsley-style derivative sovereign immunity typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and followed federal directions, which is often intertwined with the merits and therefore fails Cohen’s requirement that the issue be “completely separate from the merits,” and it is ordinarily reviewable after final judgment. See Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Constr. Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940); Van Cauwenberghe v. Biard, 486 U.S. 517, 522 (1988). Expanding interlocutory appeals here would create serious practical and institutional costs by inviting piecemeal review in a broad category of contractor cases, contrary to § 1291’s workability and this Court’s traditional restraint in enlarging collateral-order jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291’s text limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception that applies only to a small class of orders that are conclusive, resolve important issues separate from the merits, and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Under Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., an order is “effectively unreviewable” only when it vindicates a right “not to stand trial altogether,” whereas a Yearsley-based contractor defense typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization and direction—questions intertwined with the merits and often fact-bound. Because the denial of such a defense can be reviewed after final judgment and recognizing interlocutory appeals here would risk expanding collateral-order review beyond § 1291’s final-judgment rule, immediate appeal is not warranted. Will v. Hallock and Mohawk Industries reinforce that we assess the category of orders as a whole and avoid enlarging collateral-order jurisdiction absent a clear immunity-from-suit entitlement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only a narrow collateral-order exception, and a denial of Yearsley relief does not fit Cohen because it is typically intertwined with the merits and often turns on disputed facts about whether the contractor acted within “validly conferred” authority and did not “exceed” it. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940), is best understood as a defense to liability for authorized governmental work, not a free-standing immunity from being haled into court akin to sovereign or qualified immunity whose value is irretrievably lost without immediate appeal. Because the contractor’s claim can be meaningfully reviewed after final judgment, expanding interlocutory appeals here would erode § 1291’s rule and impose practical costs through delay and piecemeal litigation. Procedural fairness and access to adjudication favor keeping the case on track to resolve the merits rather than creating a new category of immediate appeal for contractor defenses.
